lesson.title: VLAN Tagging: Marking Every Frame With Its Membership
lesson.summary: VLAN tagging inserts a small extra field into an Ethernet frame that records which VLAN the frame belongs to, letting a single cable between switches carry traffic for many VLANs while keeping each one properly separated. The IEEE 802.1Q tag is what makes trunk links between switches possible.
lesson.body:
VLANs solve the broadcast domain problem beautifully within a single switch, but they raise an immediate follow up question. When two switches are connected by a single cable, and that cable needs to carry traffic for VLAN 10, VLAN 20, and VLAN 30 all at once, how does the switch on the receiving end know which VLAN each incoming frame belongs to? A plain Ethernet frame, as described earlier, has no field anywhere in its structure that records VLAN membership. Relying on which physical port a frame arrived on works fine for an end device plugged directly into one VLAN, but it breaks down completely on a shared inter switch link carrying several VLANs at once.

VLAN tagging, standardized in IEEE 802.1Q, solves this by inserting a small extra field directly into the Ethernet frame itself. This tag is four bytes long and sits right after the source MAC address, just before the EtherType field the original frame chapter described. It begins with a two byte Tag Protocol Identifier set to the value 0x8100, which signals to any switch reading the frame that a VLAN tag follows. Next comes a two byte Tag Control Information field, which itself packs together a three bit Priority Code Point used for traffic prioritization, a one bit Drop Eligible Indicator, and, most importantly, a twelve bit VLAN Identifier that can express any VLAN number from 1 to 4094. Adding these four bytes grows the maximum Ethernet frame size from the usual 1518 bytes to 1522 bytes for a tagged frame.

It helps to think in terms of tagged versus untagged frames. An ordinary end device, a laptop or a printer, has no idea VLANs exist and never generates a tag; the frames it sends are always untagged, exactly as described in the original Ethernet frame chapter. Switches are the ones that insert and remove tags, at the edges of the VLAN aware part of the network, so that end devices never need to know anything about VLAN numbers at all.

Trace a concrete frame through this process. A Sales PC, assigned to VLAN 10 on switch 1, sends a plain, untagged frame destined for a Sales file server that happens to be plugged into a port on switch 2, also in VLAN 10. Switches 1 and 2 are connected by a single inter switch link that carries traffic for VLAN 10, VLAN 20, and VLAN 30 simultaneously. When switch 1 receives the untagged frame from the PC, it knows, from the port's own VLAN assignment, that this frame belongs to VLAN 10, so it inserts an 802.1Q tag with VLAN ID 10 and sends it out across the inter switch link. Switch 2 receives the tagged frame, reads the VLAN ID field, and now knows with certainty that this frame belongs to VLAN 10, not VLAN 20 or VLAN 30, regardless of the fact that all three VLANs' traffic is mixed together on that same physical wire. Before delivering the frame out to the file server's own access port, switch 2 strips the tag back off, since the server, like the original PC, never needs to see it.

Without this tagging mechanism, two switches would have no reliable way to multiplex several VLANs' worth of traffic over a single shared link while keeping each VLAN's broadcast domain properly separate. The alternative, running one dedicated cable per VLAN between every pair of switches, would defeat much of the point of VLANs in the first place, which was to avoid needing separate physical infrastructure for every group. The 802.1Q tag is precisely what allows all of that VLAN traffic to collapse onto a single link, and the special kind of switch port built to carry exactly that mixed, tagged traffic is called a trunk port, covered next.
